description: 🚀 MayiNautas: Exploring the universe, programming the future. We are a team of four young explorers, aged 11 to 14, accompanied by our teacher, Renzo, and a parent who has joined us on this adventure. We are united by curiosity, creativity, and a desire to discover how technology can help us solve major challenges. This year, inspired by Mayito—our astronaut and programming expert—and his companion, MayiRobit, we aim to take our ideas even further.
summary: Mayi Space is a bilingual (Spanish/English) interactive game for children aged 7 to 12 that combines software and robotics. Players train as junior astronauts at the Mayi Space Station and travel through seven bases: water recycling, greenhouse, soil-free crops, zero-gravity gym, temperature control, radiation shield and dining room. At each base they face a real problem astronauts deal with, based on NASA OSDR studies, and must choose the best option to survive. Every choice has a cost: a correct answer earns resources (air, energy, shelter), while a wrong one spends them, and Mayito, our guide, explains why. If one resource reaches zero, the mission ends. A robot moves through the bases on interactive mat depending on the player’s answers, and an LED lights up when a base is completed correctly. At the end, players earn a badge and a Junior Astronaut diploma with their photo. Designed and built by kids, for kids, Mayi Space turns space science into something they can see, touch and drive, making learning creative and fun while bringing children closer to programming and robotics.
details:
What problem are we solving?

Our challenge was to create an interactive game for kids from 7 to 12 years old about surviving in space. Space content for kids is usually too simple or too hard to understand, and most kids only see the results of a mission, not the decisions astronauts have to make. We wanted kids to learn about the problems of living in space in a fun, simple and creative way, with something they can play, see and touch.

What did we build?

Mayi Space is not only an app. It has two parts that work together:

The game: you type your name and choose the time and the order of the questions. The game has a tutorial with Mayito, our guide. Then you visit the bases of the space station: water recycling, greenhouse, soil-free crops, zero-gravity gym, temperature control, radiation shield and dining room. In each base there is a real space problem, and you must choose the best option to survive. If you answer correctly, you complete the mission of that base and win resources. If you get it wrong, you spend air, power or shelter, and the game tells you why your answer was wrong. The game has 2 languages, Spanish and English.

The interactive mat and the robot: we drew and painted a mat with the bases of the space station. The robot moves through the bases depending on the player’s answers. When the player completes the mission of a base with the correct answer, an LED lights up on the map. This way, kids don’t just play on the screen: they can see their decisions come to life.

At the end, players get badges for the bases they completed correctly and a Junior Astronaut diploma where they can add their photo.

Why is it important?

It helps kids understand quickly and simply what problems astronauts have in space and how to solve them. It also brings kids closer to programming and robotics, because they can see how a game on the computer controls a real robot.

What creative elements do we use?

We used drawings, because everything we drew was very special since we made it ourselves. We drew the interactive mat where the robot moves. The robot is also a creative solution, because we are sure everyone loves driving a robot. We also used a game and slides that help people understand the problem and the solution better. Thanks to this, many boys and girls can learn about space in an easier and more fun way.

What tools, programming languages, hardware and software did we use?

Hardware: Arduino, robot, LEDs, protoboard, wires, pliers and computers.

Software: HTML, CSS and JavaScript for the game, Arduino for the LEDs and the robot, Claude, ChatGPT, Google and Firefox.

Art: colors, markers, pencils and the interactive mat.

Real NASA data

Every base is based on real NASA science: OSDR studies, DONKI solar alerts and Apollo 11 sounds from NASA.
